---
title: "Quiz: Fourier descriptors"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. An outline is the complex signal $z_n = x_n + i\,y_n$, $n = 0 \dots N-1$; its Fourier descriptors are $c_k = \frac1N\sum_n z_n e^{-2\pi i k n/N}$.

---

**Q1.** Why is it natural to use the DFT on an outline, and why are negative $k$ needed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What comes after the last point of the outline? Is $z_n$ real?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A closed outline is **periodic**: after $z_{N-1}$ comes $z_0$ again, which is exactly what the DFT assumes. The signal $z_n$ is complex, so $c_{-k}$ is not the conjugate of $c_k$ as for a real signal: both carry information. $c_k$ with $k > 0$ turns one way around the outline, $c_{-k}$ the other way; together they make an ellipse.
:::

---

**Q2.** You move an outline, double its size and turn it by 30°. What happens to $c_0$, to $c_1$ and to $|c_5|/|c_1|$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The DFT is linear; a turn multiplies every point by $e^{i\alpha}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$c_0$ (the centroid) is moved, doubled and turned with the outline. $c_1$ is multiplied by $2e^{i\pi/6}$: twice as long, turned by 30°. $|c_5|/|c_1|$ does not change: both sizes double, and the turn only changes phases.
:::

---

**Q3.** Two descriptor sets differ: $c_1$ and $c_{-1}$ are both turned by $+40°$ in the second. Was the outline turned, or started at another point?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A new start multiplies $c_k$ by $e^{2\pi i k m/N}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Turned (by 40°). A new start turns $c_k$ by an angle proportional to $k$: $c_1$ and $c_{-1}$ would turn in **opposite** directions. A turn multiplies every $c_k$ by the same $e^{i\alpha}$.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why resample a traced boundary to equal arc length before computing descriptors?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How long is one step of the boundary walk along a straight edge, and along a diagonal one?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The boundary walk takes steps of 1 pixel along straight edges and $\sqrt2$ along diagonal ones. Taking every $j$-th pixel therefore walks faster along diagonals, and this uneven speed enters every $c_k$. Turning the object changes which edges are diagonal, so a turned copy gets different descriptors and matches worse. Equal arc-length samples give every part of the outline the same weight. (The staircase of the pixels itself remains: high $k$ stay noisy.)
:::

---

**Q5.** A square is sampled at its four corners only. What do its descriptors look like, and what does that teach you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compute $c_k$ for $z = (1, i, -1, -i)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only $c_1 = 1$, all others 0: the descriptors of a circle. Four samples cannot tell a square from a circle (or from any other curve through the corners). The descriptors only know the samples, so the samples must be much denser than the detail you want to describe.
:::

---

**Q6.** Two nuclei have nearly identical $|c_k|/|c_1|$ for all $k$. Are they the same shape?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do magnitudes throw away?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not necessarily. Magnitudes lose the relative phases of the harmonics, and different arrangements of the same harmonics give different shapes with the same $|c_k|$. A mirror image (walked clockwise again) also has the same magnitudes. To be sure, match the complex descriptors (best rotation, scale and start) and look at the misfit, with the mirror allowed or not as the question requires.
:::

---

**Q7.** How does one FFT find the best starting point when matching two outlines of $N$ samples?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For a fixed start, the best rotation and scale are one complex number; how good is that fit?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For start $m$ the quality of the best fit is $|q(m)|$ with $q(m) = \sum_{k\ne0}\overline{c^A_k}\,c^B_k\,e^{-2\pi i k m/N}$: one DFT of the products $\overline{c^A_k}c^B_k$ gives all $N$ values at once (the correlation theorem: it is the circular cross-correlation of the two complex outlines). The largest $|q(m)|$ is the best start; $\lambda = q(m)/\sum|c^A_k|^2$ gives the scale $|\lambda|$ and the angle $\arg\lambda$.
:::

---

**Q8.** The match score of a nearly symmetric leaf has two high peaks, about $N/2$ starts apart. Why? And why does a mirror image never reach a score of 1 unless the mirror is allowed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a half turn do to the leaf? What can a rotation never do?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Turned by 180° and started half-way round, the leaf looks almost the same, so that start fits almost as well (the second peak, with an angle about 180° away). A mirror image cannot be produced by any rotation, scale or start (rotations keep the orientation of the walk around the shape): its best fit leaves a misfit. Allowing the mirror means also matching the conjugated outline $\overline{c_k}$ and reporting which one fitted.
:::
